name: Full-face respirators
summary: A reusable mask that seals around the whole face behind a clear visor, taking the same filters and cartridges as half masks while also covering the eyes.
uses: Same filters and cartridges as a half mask, with a higher rating when it seals: OSHA 50 against 10, UK 40 with P3 filters
Covers the eyes as well as the lungs, which helps against irritating chemicals
Asbestos and lead dust with P100 (magenta) or P3 filters; beryllium dust with P100 filters, which NIOSH lists only up to 0.01 mg/m3 (air-supplied masks above that)
Chlorine, ammonia, solvents or mercury vapour only with the matching cartridge, changed before it is spent
Ordinary cartridges don't stop carbon monoxide, and no filter mask works in oxygen-poor air: silos, tanks, pits, sewers, wells, fires
Glasses with side arms, beards and stubble under the seal let air in round the edge
identify: A rubber or silicone mask with a large clear visor over eyes, nose and mouth, an inner mask, a head harness, an outlet valve and one or two filter ports (HSE HSG53); European ones are made to EN 136 (HSE HSG53). Cartridges use the same colours as half masks. US: black organic vapour, white acid gas, green ammonia, yellow organic vapour plus acid gas, magenta P100 (OSHA bulletin; CDPR colours). For multi-gas the sources differ: OSHA's bulletin lists brown for acid gas, organic vapour and ammonia together and olive for multi-contaminant, while California's chart gives olive/brown, so go by the protections printed on the cartridge, not its colour. Europe: brown A, grey B (not for carbon monoxide), yellow E, green K, red-and-white Hg, white P (HSE HSG53). The approval label is a paper sheet in the box listing the mask, cartridges and parts approved together, with TC-23C numbers for gas sets and TC-84A for particle or combination sets; parts not on it can cause serious injury or death (NIOSH approval labels). Fake cartridges are sold, so check each shows the maker, part number, protection type, NIOSH and a lot number (NIOSH counterfeit cartridges). OSHA rates a full facepiece at 50, five times a half mask (OSHA 1910.134). Its fit-test appendix sets a pass of 500 for a full facepiece, and the simple taste or smell test is allowed only for masks needing a fit factor of 100 or less, so the 50 rating needs an instrument fit test (OSHA 1910.134; OSHA fit test appendix). The UK rates it 40 with P3 filters and 20 with gas filters (HSE HSG53). A mask fed from an air cylinder or compressor (breathing apparatus, such as SCBA) is a different kind of equipment, not a filter mask: it needs a supply of breathing-quality air (HSE HSG53) and training.
test: Inspect before each use: facepiece soft and springy with no cracks, tears or sticky patches; visor not cracked; every strap and buckle working; valves present, flat and seated, since perished or warped valves can't seal (OSHA 1910.134; HSE HSG53). Fit identical filters to both ports (HSE HSG53). Use gas cartridges from air-tight packs within their date: OSHA says even cartridges in their original packaging have expiry dates, and open ones, or ones not in air-tight packaging, should not be used (OSHA bulletin). Particle filters past their expiry date should not be used either (HSE HSG53). Seal check every time: palms over the inlets, breathe in gently so the mask pulls in, hold about 10 seconds and it must stay in; then cover the outlet valve and breathe out gently: pressure should build up slightly inside the mask with no air leaking out at the edge (OSHA seal check). Facial hair under the seal breaks it (OSHA 1910.134; CCOHS selection), and so do glasses: spectacles with side arms break a full-face seal, and makers supply special frames that fit inside the mask (HSE HSG53). A seal check is not a fit test (NIOSH FFR page). Change gas cartridges on a schedule, not by smell (OSHA change schedules): HSE suggests class 1 at least every two days, class 2 weekly, Hg after 50 hours, AX after one use, and at once if you smell or taste anything (HSE HSG53). After use, clean and disinfect it and store it away from sun, heat, damp, dust and chemicals, packed so the facepiece and valves don't warp (OSHA 1910.134).

decay.note: Estimate: NIOSH's example gives a reusable facepiece ten years and a particle filter five (NIOSH shelf life); no maker figure for cartridges was found. OSHA says cartridges carry expiry dates and opened ones shouldn't be used (OSHA bulletin), so cartridges run out first.

improvise: No full-face mask: a half mask plus goggles is the nearest substitute, with a lower rating (10 against 50), as long as the goggles don't break the mask's seal (OSHA 1910.134). For dust only, a P100 or FFP3 disposable with goggles; disposables don't stop gas or vapour (NIOSH FFR page). Not for asbestos work, where OSHA bars filtering facepieces (OSHA asbestos), and not for beryllium, where the NIOSH Pocket Guide lists no disposable (NIOSH beryllium guide). Where eye protection matters most: OSHA's lead rule calls for a full facepiece where lead dust would irritate the eyes (OSHA lead), and the NIOSH Pocket Guide lists full-face masks or better for beryllium dust (NIOSH beryllium guide). Glasses with side arms break the seal of a full-face mask; makers supply special frames that fit inside it (HSE HSG53; CCOHS selection). Bearded: shave the seal line; only loose-fitting hooded respirators, usually battery-powered, work with beards (CDC fit testing; NIOSH construction dust). Nothing improvised replaces a gas cartridge; even a real one gives no protection once full, and its life is hard to predict (HSE HSG53). A full face does not make a dangerous space safe. No filter mask works in oxygen-poor air, so stay out of silos, manure pits, tanks, sewers, wells and burning buildings (HSE HSG53; Alberta producers). Ordinary cartridges don't stop carbon monoxide: NIOSH lists supplied air, or a gas mask with a special canister for CO, which you are unlikely to find (NIOSH CO guide; OSHA bulletin). In a fire, get out; don't go in.
